title: The sea ice around Antarctica grows about sixfold every winter
body: Each southern autumn and winter, the ocean around Antarctica freezes outward from the coast. The ice grows from about **3 million km²** in February to about **18 million km²** in September, roughly the area of the continent itself, and most of it melts again the next summer. It is mostly first-year ice, generally less than a few metres thick, and how far it spreads is largely set by the winds and currents that push it north. In 2024 it grew from 1.99 to 17.16 million km², the [second-lowest winter peak on record](https://svs.gsfc.nasa.gov/5391/).

slides.heading: Salt squeezed out
slides.text: Sea ice is mostly fresh. As seawater freezes, the salt is pushed out into the water below, making it dense enough to sink. That sinking, salty water plays a key role in forming Antarctic Bottom Water in the deep ocean.

slides.question: What mostly sets how far north the ice spreads?
slides.explanation: Antarctic sea ice extent is largely controlled by the winds and currents that push the ice northwards, away from the coast.
